sources.title: Edgar Thurston, assisted by K. Rangachari, Castes and Tribes of Southern India, Volume II (Government Press, Madras,1909)
sources.locator: Gaudo entry printed273–276; especially273–274. Adjacent Gauda entry269 explicitly distinguishes Canarese and Oriya uses. Web lines2484–2500.
claims: Entry quotes1891/1901Madras census describing Ganjam Oriya Gaudos as cattle breeders, while many northern-district members already cultivated. Date this evidence; northern districts is source wording, not automatically all modern northern Odisha.
Quotation from1871census describes buffaloes raised on hill pastures and valued by low-country cartmen for draught; source is1909quotation, not separately verified1871volume.
Author questions reported subdivisions: Behara apparently a title and Pattilia probably mistake for Pachilia. Useful evidence that historical classifications themselves require scrutiny.
Sollokhondia subsection describes agriculture, cattle/sheep and cart-driving, alongside hereditary council officers; applies to that historical regional subsection.
Gopopuriya and Madhurapuriya names connected to legendary origin history. Yadava/Krishna descent explicitly self-reported tradition, not genealogy.
limits: Colonial outsider classification contains hierarchy and stereotypes; do not reproduce those as truth.
Do not turn listed subdivisions into validated contemporary branches or automatically equate similarly spelled Karnataka groups.
No founder/date or ethnic antiquity established.
Original1909 publication is historical witness; source prose budget conservatively200 even though old publication.

sources.title: Ganjam District Gazetteer, Gauda subsection
claims: Gauda described as cattle rearers and sellers of milk/products, some changing occupations for better living.
Names Gopal, Gopa, Goala, Golla, Ahir, Idalya in different parts of India; this is its comparison, not proof of universal community equivalence.
Krishna/Yadava descent as community tradition, Dola Purnima major festival, ceremonial cattle worship and Radha-Krishna songs.
limits: Publication/compilation date unresolved in this check; URLuploaddate is not publicationdate.
Use Gopala/Gauda connection only in Odishan context and attributed source scope.

sources.title: Bhadrak District Gazetteer, Gauda subsection
claims: Distinguishes Mathura-puria, Gopapuria and Magadha in quotation from OMalley; preserve historical provenance and reject ranking.
Colonialquoted account describes women preparing curd/ghee and elder women selling dairy products; not contemporary occupational statistics.
Dola Purnima associated with Gauda but explicitly celebrated by other communities too.
limits: Sweeping assertion differences disappeared through education is not independent contemporary evidence.
No equivalence to adjacent Chasa/Dagara sections.
Edition2015–16 compilation context from existing dossier; exactimprint not independently established here.

sources.status: original passage read from parent capture
claims: Attributes Gopalanka Ogala to Achyutananda; describes conversational themes Radha-Krishna, flute, stick, rope, Vrindavan, buffalo horn and peacock feather.
Describes milkmen singing these themes while filling water pitchers during Dola Purnima.
limits: 2012literary interpretation, not direct manuscript dating or recorded fieldwork.
Avoid claims first patron, founder, caste ancestry of poet, universal current practice or exactmedievalorigin.

narrative_plan: Open with cattle work and community memory, carefully bounded Odishan naming rather than universal synonyms.
Dated1909 record shows agriculture already alongside husbandry; buffalo and cart links demonstrate practical regional economy.
Show records themselves unstable: title versus subdivision; regional differences require specific investigation.
Ganjam/Bhadrak Dola and Krishna devotion connect livelihood with remembered identity; festival not exclusive.
Concrete Ogala water-pitcher performance and Nemalo Laudi provide literary/performance heritage with attributed evidence.
Close with honest unanswered formation question and changing occupations, not extinction narrative.
